title: Do women have to cover in front of homosexuals or transgender individuals?
headline: Schools tie a person's covering rules to birth sex and the risk of description

summary.text: The four schools address the nearest classical cases, the effeminate man, the person of ambiguous sex, and the non-Muslim or corrupt woman, and the contemporary fatwas transfer those rulings to homosexual and trans-identified persons. Hanafi muftis and AMJA require a woman to cover before homosexual men and women as before non-mahram men, while a Darul Ifta answer holds that transition does not change a person's sex or its rulings. The schools differ mainly over the scope of the concession in Quran 24:31, not over its logic.

paragraphs.text: The obligation is framed first as restraint of the gaze and guarding chastity, before any list of relatives: "Tell the believing men to reduce [some] of their vision and guard their private parts" (Quran 24:30). The parallel verse for women sets out the exceptions to uncovering adornment, among them "their women" and "those male attendants having no physical desire" (Quran 24:31).

A third verse gives the general purpose, that the outer garment makes a woman "known and not be abused" (Quran 33:59), and a fourth relaxes the outer garment only for elderly women past marriage who "have no desire for marriage," and even then prefers modesty (Quran 24:60). The Quran also treats clothing itself as a sign, with "the clothing of righteousness" named as best (Quran 7:26).

The dispute turns on the phrase "their women" (nisāʾihinn). Ibn Abbas read it as Muslim women only, and held it unlawful for a Muslim woman to uncover before a Jew or Christian "lest she describe her to her husband," a reading also reported from Mujahid, Makhul and Ibn Jurayj. Umar ibn al-Khattab acted on that reading, writing to Abu Ubaydah to stop non-Muslim women entering the bathhouses with Muslim women.

Against this, Aisha's own practice is cited, that Jewish women used to enter upon the Prophet's wives without them veiling, and Ibn Arabi al-Maliki is reported as holding the correct view to be that it covers all women. Al-Razi in Tafsir al-Kabir records both and says the second is the adopted opinion, with the salaf's strictness carried on istihbab rather than obligation. Al-Uthaymeen likewise called the permissive reading "the closest view," while al-Albani took the restrictive one and said a non-Muslim woman is "like a man" in relation to a Muslim woman.

Bukhari records the effeminate man (mukhannath) who used to enter upon the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, counted among "those without desire," until he described a woman's body and the Prophet ﷺ said: "This man must not enter upon you women." (Sahih al-Bukhari 5235) In Abu Dawud's wording Aisha reports: "Do I not see that this man knows what goes on here? Let him not enter upon you again," and they kept him out (graded Sahih). A third narration has the command "Remove them from your houses" (graded Sahih).

The prohibition on imitating the opposite sex is firmly established: the Prophet ﷺ "cursed the woman who imitates men and the man who imitates women" (Sunan Ibn Majah 1903, Hasan Sahih), and the same in Sunan Abi Dawud 4097 (Sahih) and Ibn Majah 1904 (Sahih). The reason describing matters: "A woman should not be in physical contact with another woman and then describe her to her husband as if he were looking at her" (Sahih al-Bukhari 5240, Sahih). And more broadly, no woman removes her clothes anywhere but her husband's house "except that she has torn down the veil between herself and her Lord" (Jami' at-Tirmidhi 2803, graded hasan).

The Ansar women's response to the veil verses, tearing their waist-wrappers to cover their heads, is Sahih (Sunan Abi Dawud 4101). The report that the Prophet ﷺ told Umm Salamah and Maymunah to veil from the blind Ibn Umm Maktum, asking "Are you two blind?", is graded Daif by al-Albani with an isnad hasan by Zubair Ali Zai in Sunan Abi Dawud 4112, while Riyad as-Salihin records Tirmidhi's grading of hasan sahih for it. Abu Dawud himself appended that this was specific to the wives of the Prophet ﷺ.

The schools' books do not use the word "homosexual" as a social category; they address the mukhannath, the khuntha mushkil and, for women, the corrupt or non-Muslim woman. The Hanafi Radd al-Muhtar distinguishes the mukhannath who imitates women by choice and lets others use him from one with natural softness who does not desire women, and some Hanafi sheikhs allowed the latter to be present with women. Fatawa Mahmudiyya holds that the "tabi'un without desire" may see a young woman in a thick chemise and headcover, but not her hair or skin.

Radd al-Muhtar and Fath al-Qadir treat a dhimmi woman as like a non-mahram man, and hold that woman with woman normally sees what a man sees of a man, navel to knee. The Maliki Hashiyat al-Dassuqi says the bar on the non-Muslim woman is "for an incidental reason, not because she is awrah," namely that she may describe her, and that a woman with a free non-Muslim woman may see everything except face and hands.

The Shafi'i Mughni al-Muhtaj treats the khuntha mushkil with the stricter rule: counted a man among women and a woman among men. Rawdat al-Talibin reports two views on the castrated man and the mukhannath, the one whose desire has gone being treated as a mahram, while al-Zarkashi restricted that concession to a Muslim castrated man; if non-Muslim, he is barred.

Al-Mughni holds that whoever's desire has gone, including the mukhannath without desire, takes the ruling of a mahram; but if he has desire and knows women's affairs he is like any other man, citing Aisha's hadith. Kashshaf al-Qina' holds that the khuntha mushkil of ten or more years must cover more than the navel-to-knee area, since his femininity is unverified.

On the modern cases, Hanafi muftis state that women must cover before homosexuals and trans-identified individuals exactly as before heterosexual men, with no difference at all, and the same for castrated males. The Assembly of Muslim Jurists of America rules that an adult Muslim woman must be fully covered before a homosexual woman, keeping interaction minimal because of the risk of seduction, and that the same applies with a gay man, "as he is a male and has the sexual lust others have, even if he is a homosexual." IslamQA answers the question about a gay man by noting that covering face and hands before non-mahram men is required, and that before a known evildoer it is more emphatically so.

On "their women," the reconciliation offered by those who permit is that the restriction was tied to its reason, the fear that a non-Muslim woman would describe the Muslim woman to men who could pursue her, so where that fear is absent the restriction lapses. This is stated explicitly in the Maliki gloss, by IslamQA, and by AMJA, which says anyone who might describe what they see takes the ruling of a marriageable man "regardless of his/her gender, age, religion, blood relationship." IslamQA adds that the strict view is nonetheless a valid position with sound support, and that a woman may adopt it out of caution without censuring those who differ.

On the mukhannath, the verse names those "without desire" as an exception, yet the Prophet ﷺ expelled the mukhannath of Bukhari 5235 once he demonstrated he understood women's bodies. Ibn Qudama resolves this by treating the phrase as a description of a condition, not a permanent label: the concession belongs to the man in whom desire is genuinely absent, and the moment he shows knowledge of women's affairs "his ruling is the ruling of others." Ibn Abidin makes the same move from the Hanafi side, separating natural softness from deliberate imitation.

On the person of ambiguous or altered sex, the Shafi'i rule is to apply the stricter of the two rulings in matters of exposure, and IslamOnline reaches the same conclusion for the unresolved case, avoiding privacy with either sex until the state is medically settled. Where a person has transitioned, the resolution is that the birth sex governs the rulings while outward resemblance calls for precaution.

The International Islamic Fiqh Academy's 2023 decision (no. 251) holds that changing sex is forbidden as a change to Allah's creation, citing the verse reporting Satan's promise to command such change (Quran 4:119) and the hadith of cursing those who imitate the opposite sex, and that a spouse may seek dissolution if the other transitions. The Muslim World League's earlier 1989 resolution drew the same line but allowed surgical correction where a trustworthy doctor establishes buried physical signs of the other sex, treating it as medical treatment rather than transition. AMJA states that transsexualism is absolutely forbidden and cites the curse hadith.

A Darul Ifta answer holds that since neither surgery nor hormones genuinely change a person's sex, "a transgender individual who undergoes either or both procedures remains the same sex and the rulings of that sex continue to apply," with some precautionary rules because of outward resemblance. On the intersex case, IslamOnline explains that the classical khuntha is returned to one of the two sexes by physical signs, and that the unresolved case should not be alone with men or with women until specialists settle the matter.
